name: Write and Forget Policies
question: What should be saved, and when must it go?
summary: Rules for what becomes memory, how duplicates and conflicts are merged, and when memories expire. Forgetting covers decay, time-to-live limits and user deletion, which must reach every copy: database rows, vectors, summaries and caches. Under India’s DPDP Act, erasure on request or when the purpose ends is a legal duty.
useCases: Any long-term memory that holds personal data
Stores that grow without limit or keep contradicting themselves

items.detail: only named categories are saved: preferences, contact channel, goals
never store OTPs, card numbers, Aadhaar, PAN or health data in memory
newer wins; older is invalidated with a date, not silently kept
one-off items expire; unused items fade
delete rows, vectors, summaries and caches; log that it happened
write immediately (latency) or in a scheduled job (cheaper)
DPDP Act right to erasure: remove the person from rows, vectors, summaries, caches and backups on a schedule, then confirm

steps: Allow-list categories and block sensitive patterns before anything is written
Save only stable, reusable facts; skip one-off remarks
Consolidate conflicts and attach a time-to-live per category
Delete everywhere on request, log it, and audit a sample weekly
pitfalls: Deleting database rows but leaving embeddings and summaries behind
Storing OTPs or identity numbers because they appeared in a chat
Keeping both the old and new address with no validity dates
Treating erasure as a one-off script instead of a tested job with a deletion log that holds IDs, not the data
remember: Save less. Delete everywhere. Keep the proof.
caption: Illustrative. Legal points are summaries of the DPDP Act and Rules, not legal advice.

comparison.needs: Policy, filters, deletion jobs, audit log

code.text: def write(uid, c):                     # c: category, text, stability 0-1
if c.category not in ALLOW or any(re.search(p, c.text, re.I) for p in BLOCK):
if c.stability < 0.7:              # a remark, not a reusable fact
for old in db.find(uid, category=c.category, valid=True):
expires = now + TTL[c.category] if c.category in TTL else None
row = db.insert(uid, c, valid=True, created=now, expires=expires)
bad = [r for r in db.sample(n) if any(re.search(p, r.text, re.I) for p in BLOCK)]

steps.title: Allow-list and block
steps.text: Only named categories may be written, and patterns for OTPs, PAN, Aadhaar and card numbers are blocked before anything reaches a store.

steps.title: Save stable facts only
steps.text: “Prefers Hindi” is reusable; “asked the gold rate today” is not. A stability score below 0.7 means skip.

steps.title: Consolidate conflicts
steps.text: A new address invalidates the old one with a date instead of sitting beside it. History stays for audit; retrieval sees only valid facts.

steps.title: Attach TTLs
steps.text: One-off complaints expire after 30 days. Unused items can also decay, so the store does not grow forever.

steps.title: Delete everywhere
steps.text: An erasure removes rows, vectors, rolling summaries and caches. One audit line records that it happened, without the data.

steps.title: Audit weekly
steps.text: Sample stored memories for blocked patterns, expired items still present and deletions with no audit line.

pros: Keeps memory small, current and lawful
Stops sensitive data at the door
cons: Pattern filters miss paraphrased sensitive data
Deleting every derived copy needs careful bookkeeping
Too strict a policy forgets useful facts
Retention rules differ by law and sector
avoidWhen: There is no long-term memory, only one session
Records the law requires you to keep (keep them in the system of record, not agent memory)

playgroundGuide.scenario: A bank’s assistant proposes 10 candidate memories from recent chats, each with a stability score: three preferences, an OTP, a PAN number, a hospital visit, an old and a new address, a one-off app crash and a question about the gold rate. The store is shown 90 days later, and the customer may file a DPDP erasure request.
controls: Set the save threshold on the stability score.
Toggle the sensitive-data filter and a 30-day TTL for one-off items, and choose how conflicts are handled.
Request erasure and choose how far deletion reaches: rows, rows and vectors, or every copy.

outputs.name: Sensitive items stored
outputs.meaning: OTP, PAN or health data in memory.

outputs.name: Stale items
outputs.meaning: An old address still marked valid, or one-off items kept forever.

outputs.name: Copies surviving erasure
outputs.meaning: Rows, vectors, summary and cache copies left after an erasure request.

presets.name: Save almost everything
presets.expect: Threshold 0.30: 9 of 10 stored, including 3 sensitive items, with 2 stale (old address and the app crash).

presets.name: Threshold 0.70
presets.expect: 7 stored, all 3 preferences, but the PAN number and hospital visit still get in: stability is not sensitivity.

presets.name: Filter plus 0.85 threshold
presets.expect: 0 sensitive and 0 stale, but only 2 of 3 preferences survive: too strict.

presets.name: Erase rows only
presets.expect: The erasure deletes 9 rows but 11 copies survive: 9 vectors, the summary and the cache.

missions.text: Store 0 sensitive items while keeping all 3 preferences.
missions.hint: No threshold does this alone: the PAN scores 0.88, above “No SMS alerts” at 0.80.

missions.text: After an erasure request, leave 0 copies outside the audit log.
missions.hint: Rows are not enough. Delete vectors, the summary and the cache as well.

missions.text: Reach 0 stale items with all 3 preferences kept.
missions.hint: Let the newer address win, and expire or skip one-off items.

tools.best: One API for adding, updating, deleting and deleting all memories per user.
tools.ex: delete_all(user_id=...) on an erasure request, then log the event.
pros: Deletion reaches the memory store and its vectors
cons: Summaries and caches outside Mem0 are yours

tools.best: Invalidating contradicted facts with validity windows while keeping history.
tools.ex: The old address gets an end date when the new one arrives; retrieval uses only valid facts.
cons: Erasure must still remove history for personal data

tools.best: Background agents that consolidate and rewrite memory between conversations.
tools.ex: A nightly sleep-time agent merges duplicate facts and drops expired one-offs.

tools.best: Background memory managers that consolidate and update stored memories.
tools.ex: Run the memory manager after each session to merge updates into the profile.

tools.best: Detecting and redacting PII in text before it is written anywhere.
tools.ex: Add custom recognizers for PAN and Aadhaar formats and block writes that match.

quickPicks.tool: Mem0 delete_all plus your own caches

goals: Design an allow-list and block-list for what may become memory
Handle conflicts and expiry so memory stays current
List every copy an erasure must reach and how to prove it happened

practice.scenario: A bank’s assistant receives a DPDP erasure request. The memory service deletes the customer’s preference rows, the matching vectors, the rolling summary and the cached profile, and writes one audit line. Records that KYC and tax law require are kept in the core systems, not in the assistant’s memory, and a nightly job drops one-off items past their time-to-live.

industries.use: Block OTPs, card numbers and Aadhaar from memory; erase on request
Keep appointment preferences, never diagnoses, in assistant memory
Expire one-off complaints; keep size and delivery preferences

practice.analogy: A records room with a retention schedule. Only listed document types are filed, each has a shred date, and every shredding is logged.

library.name: Mem0
library.what: Memory layer with add, update, delete and delete_all per user, so writes and erasure go through one API.

practice.note: drop_summaries, drop_cache and audit stand for your own stores. Regex filters are a first line only; add a PII detector such as Presidio.

numericDrill.question: A user’s data sits in 4 table rows, 4 vectors, 1 rolling summary and 1 cache entry. Deletion removes only the table rows. What fraction of the copies survive, as a percentage?

interview.question: What should never go into an assistant’s long-term memory?
interview.answer: OTPs, passwords, card numbers, Aadhaar and PAN, and health details, unless there is a clear lawful purpose and controls. Save only allow-listed, stable, reusable categories, and filter before writing.

interview.question: What does honouring an erasure request involve for an AI assistant?
interview.answer: Deleting every copy of the personal data it holds: rows, embeddings, summaries, caches and backups on their schedule, while keeping records other laws require in the system of record, and logging the erasure.

mistakes.mistake: Deleting table rows but not embeddings or summaries
mistakes.fix: Track every derived copy and delete them together

mistakes.mistake: Saving everything and filtering at read time
mistakes.fix: Filter and classify before anything is written

quiz.question: A customer asks the bank assistant to erase their data. Engineering deletes the memory rows. What is still wrong?
options: Vectors, summaries and caches may still hold the data
The audit log must also be deleted
quiz.explanation: Erasure must reach every derived copy; a minimal audit line without the data is kept as proof.

quiz.question: Which should never be written to an assistant’s long-term memory? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: OTPs and card numbers must be blocked; language and channel preferences are useful, safe facts.

quiz.question: A policyholder’s old and new addresses are both stored as valid. What policy fixes this?
options: Keep both; the model will choose
Newer wins; the older is invalidated with a date
quiz.explanation: Consolidating conflicts keeps one current fact and history for audit.

quiz.question: A user’s data sits in 4 rows, 4 vectors, 1 summary and 1 cache entry. Deletion removes only the rows. What percentage of copies survive?
quiz.explanation: Copies: 10. Surviving: 6. 6 ÷ 10 = 60%.

quiz.question: Under India’s DPDP Act, section 8(7), when must a data fiduciary erase personal data?
options: Never, if it might be useful
When consent is withdrawn or the purpose is no longer served, unless law requires retention
Only when a court orders it
quiz.explanation: Section 8(7) requires erasure on withdrawal of consent or when the purpose ends, subject to legal retention. This is a summary, not legal advice.

quiz.question: “App crashed on login” is saved as a memory. What should happen to it?
options: Give it a TTL so it expires, for example after 30 days
Promote it to the system prompt
quiz.explanation: One-off items should expire so the store does not fill with stale noise.

quiz.question: Which are sound parts of a memory write policy? Select all that apply.
options: Pattern and PII filters before writing
Saving everything and filtering at read time
Keeping contradictory facts with no dates
quiz.explanation: Allow-lists and pre-write filters work; read-time filtering still stores the data, and undated contradictions cause stale answers.

quiz.question: DPDP Rules 2025 require processing logs to be kept for at least how long?
quiz.explanation: Rule 8 requires the logs to be kept for at least one year. This is a summary, not legal advice.

quiz.question: LangGraph describes two times to write memory. Which is the trade-off of writing in the hot path?
options: It is immediate but adds latency to the response
quiz.explanation: Hot-path writes are available immediately but add latency; background writes are cheaper but delayed.

quiz.question: Ten candidates arrive; 3 are sensitive, 2 are one-offs and 1 is an outdated address. With filters, a stability threshold and conflict handling, how many valid memories remain?
quiz.explanation: 10 − 3 sensitive − 2 one-offs − 1 outdated = 4 valid memories.

quiz.question: A patient requests erasure. Which must the system delete? Select all that apply.
options: The audit line recording that the erasure happened
quiz.explanation: Rows, embeddings and summaries are copies. The audit line, without the data, is proof of deletion.

quiz.question: A stability threshold of 0.8 blocks an OTP scored 0.6 but lets a PAN scored 0.88 through. What is the lesson?
options: Stability is not sensitivity; add a sensitive-data filter
quiz.explanation: Sensitive items can look stable; they need a separate filter.

quiz.question: What do Letta sleep-time agents do?
options: Consolidate and rewrite memory in the background
Delete all memories after a session
quiz.explanation: Sleep-time agents modify memory asynchronously, between conversations.

quiz.question: A regex blocks 12-digit numbers to stop Aadhaar numbers being stored. What does it miss?
options: Numbers written with spaces or in words, and other identifiers
quiz.explanation: Pattern filters are a first line; add a PII detector such as Presidio and allow-lists.

quiz.question: An erasure removes rows and vectors but not the rolling summary or cache. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The data can still reach the model through the summary
The cache may serve the old profile
Only an audit line should remain after erasure
quiz.explanation: Leftover summaries and caches keep the data retrievable; only an audit line should remain.

quiz.question: A bank must keep KYC records by law but has received an erasure request for the assistant’s memory. What is the right design?
options: Keep KYC records in the system of record; erase the assistant’s memory copies
Move the KYC records into assistant memory
quiz.explanation: Legal retention applies to the system of record; agent memory should not hold those records.

quiz.question: Stored memories: 9 items with a row and a vector each, plus 1 summary and 1 cache. How many copies exist?
What should a weekly memory audit check?
options: Blocked patterns present, expired items still stored, deletions without audit lines
quiz.explanation: Audits verify that the policy is enforced.

quiz.question: Which are valid forgetting mechanisms? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: TTLs, decay and deletion are forgetting mechanisms; duplication makes forgetting harder.

quiz.question: Under DPDP Rule 8, how much notice must be given before erasure after the Third Schedule period ends?
quiz.explanation: Rule 8 requires 48 hours’ notice before erasure. This is a summary, not legal advice.
